design_detail: Modelling study (comparative risk assessment, called population-based by the authors). Levin-based population attributable fractions (PAFs) by country, sex, age group and cancer site combine the modelled distribution of intake among current drinkers (integrated from 0.1 to 150 g/day) with relative-risk functions for current drinking from the WCRF Continuous Update Project, against a theoretical minimum-risk exposure of lifetime abstention. Exposure is WHO GISAH adult per-capita consumption in 2010 (assumed 10-year latency); outcome is GLOBOCAN 2020 cancer incidence for the cancers with sufficient evidence in IARC monograph 100E: lip and oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only), colon, rectum, liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only), larynx and female breast. Uncertainty from 1000 Monte Carlo-like draws. Former drinking, and stomach and pancreatic cancer, enter only sensitivity analyses. Design choice per the round's brief: attributable-burden estimates are filed as 'modelling' with no validated instrument.
can_establish: How many new cancer cases in 2020, by country, region, sex, site and level of intake, are attributable to alcohol if the model's inputs and assumptions hold: causal relative risks from the WCRF reviews applied to every population, 2010 exposure with a 10-year lag, current drinking only, and lifetime abstention as the counterfactual.
cannot_establish: Whether alcohol causes these cancers (taken as given from IARC); the burden under other assumptions about risk at low intake, latency, former drinking, or interaction with tobacco and hepatitis viruses (only two sensitivity analyses are run); alcohol-attributable deaths (incidence only); or the net effect of alcohol on all cancers, since the inverse kidney association is deliberately left out.

sample.recruitment: No participants. Inputs: GLOBOCAN 2020 country-specific incidence estimates (IARC) for the selected sites and for all cancers excluding non-melanoma skin cancer; the histological split of oesophageal cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, from Arnold et al., 2020) and of liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, unpublished estimates by the first author); WHO GISAH adult per-capita consumption in 2010 by age group (15–19, 20–24, 25–34, 35–49, 50–64, 65 and older) and sex, combining recorded, unrecorded and tourist consumption; relative risks for current drinking from the WCRF Continuous Update Project systematic reviews (Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st–3rd paragraphs). The relative-risk values and the exposure model are in the appendix (pp 2–5, 7–8), which was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cancer sites with sufficient evidence of causation in IARC monograph 100E. Oesophageal and liver cancer restricted to squamous cell and hepatocellular carcinoma. Stomach and pancreatic cancer (causal in WCRF but not IARC classifications) only in sensitivity analysis. The probable protective association with kidney cancer at intakes up to 30 g/day (WCRF) was not included, because the aim was to count avoidable cancers. Ten countries without alcohol prevalence data were given their region's average age-, sex- and site-specific PAFs (Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st paragraph; Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: All countries in GLOBOCAN 2020, grouped into 17 UN world regions and into Human Development Index categories; exposure modelled for ages 15 and over.
sample.selection_effects: The quality of per-capita and survey data varies between countries and is most open to bias where unrecorded consumption is large or no nationally representative survey exists (Discussion, 6th paragraph). GLOBOCAN incidence is itself estimated for countries without high-quality registries, and the 2020 figures do not reflect COVID-19 disruptions to diagnosis (Discussion, 8th paragraph). The site list follows IARC, so only cancers with an established causal link are counted.

exposure.measurement: Population-level exposure: 2010 adult per-capita consumption (litres of pure alcohol per year, converted to g/day) from recorded, unrecorded and tourist consumption, used to correct survey-based intake for under-reporting; prevalence of current drinking and the distribution of intake among current drinkers by age, sex and country follow the method of Shield and colleagues (appendix pp 3–4, not read). The authors state that the correction does not allow for different under-reporting by age and sex or for changes in consumption before and after 2010, and that surveys underestimate the prevalence of former drinking (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average daily intake among current drinkers, integrated from 0.1 to 150 g/day (the PAF formula as rendered; Statistical analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Categories: moderate below 20 g/day (described as up to two drinks a day), risky 20–60 g/day (two to six drinks) and heavy above 60 g/day (more than six drinks), which implies a 10-g drink; also 10-g/day bands from below 10 up to 140–150 g/day. One year's exposure (2010) stands for the exposure behind 2020 incidence; drinking histories and patterns are not modelled.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is not modelled: there is no alcohol–tobacco interaction, and the authors state that residual confounding by tobacco in the relative risks may mean some alcohol-attributable cases were caused by tobacco. Synergy with hepatitis B or C virus, aflatoxin and obesity for liver cancer is not considered either (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former drinkers (lifetime use but none in the past 12 months) carry no excess risk in the main analysis; a sensitivity analysis gives them sex-specific relative risks from several sources (Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Counterfactual (theoretical minimum-risk exposure): lifetime abstention from alcohol for the whole population (Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The same relative risks are applied in every country; the authors say this may underestimate the burden where risk is higher, for example in East Asian carriers of the ALDH2*2 allele and in people with a history of cancer, and that high-quality cohort studies in low- and middle-income settings are scarce (Discussion, 7th paragraph). The reference group behind the WCRF relative risks (lifetime abstainers, all non-drinkers, or lowest intake) is not stated in the main text.

outcomes.instruments: GLOBOCAN 2020 incidence by ICD-10: lip and oral cavity (C00–C06), pharynx (C09–C10, C12–C13), oesophagus (C15; attributable cases from squamous cell carcinoma, ICD-O-3 8050–8078 and 8083–8084), colon (C18), rectum (C19–C20), liver (C22; attributable cases from hepatocellular carcinoma, ICD-O-3 8170–8175), larynx (C32), female breast (C50), and all cancers excluding non-melanoma skin cancer (C00–C97 excluding C44) (Table and footnotes).
outcomes.validity_norms: GLOBOCAN figures are themselves modelled for many countries. The hepatocellular carcinoma split comes from unpublished estimates, said to represent 80% of primary liver cancers (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Alcohol-attributable new cases = PAF × incident cases, by age, sex, country and site; age-standardised incidence rates per 100,000. For oesophageal and liver cancer the attributable cases are computed from squamous cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, but the PAF is expressed as a fraction of all oesophageal and all liver cancers (Table footnotes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive model estimates with uncertainty intervals, no hypothesis tests.

analysis.effect_sizes: All counts are model estimates of new cases in 2020 attributable to alcohol against lifetime abstention, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs). Global: 741,300 (558,500–951,200), PAF 4.1% (3.1–5.3) of all new cancers; men 568,700 (422,500–731,100), PAF 6.1% (4.6–7.9); women 172,600 (135,900–220,100), PAF 2.0% (1.6–2.5); age-standardised rate 8.4 (6.2–10.9) per 100,000 (men 13.4, women 3.7). By site, cases (PAF): oesophagus 189,700 (31.6%), liver 154,700 (17.3%), breast 98,300 (4.4%), colon 91,500 (8.1%), lip and oral cavity 74,900 (20.2%), rectum 65,100 (9.0%), pharynx 39,400 (22.0%), larynx 27,600 (15.0%). By intake: heavy (above 60 g/day) 346,400 (46.7%; 227,900–489,400), risky (20–60 g/day) 291,800 (39.4%; 227,700–333,100), moderate (below 20 g/day) 103,100 (13.9%; 82,600–207,200); up to 10 g/day 41,300 (35,400–145,800). Regions: PAF lowest in northern Africa (0.3%, 0.1–3.3) and western Asia (0.7%, 0.5–1.2), highest in eastern Asia (5.7%, 3.6–7.9) and central and eastern Europe (5.6%, 4.6–6.6). Sensitivity analyses: adding stomach and pancreatic cancer gives 808,700 (616,300–1,034,800; PAF 4.5%); adding former drinking gives 925,900 (705,900–1,187,500; PAF 5.2%).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; inputs are stratified by age group, sex and country.
analysis.selective_reporting: Country-level and most regional results, the relative-risk functions, the exposure model and the regional breakdown by intake category are in the appendix (not read). Site-specific results of the two sensitivity analyses are 'data not shown'. Figures 1–4 are images whose values were not extracted. Code and input files are available only on request to the corresponding author (Data sharing).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under the model's assumptions (lifetime abstention as the counterfactual, WCRF relative risks applied in every country, 2010 exposure with a 10-year lag, current drinking only), about 741,000 (UI 559,000–951,000), or 4.1%, of new cancers worldwide in 2020 are attributable to alcohol; three quarters are in men, 86% come from intake of 20 g/day or more, 103,100 (82,600–207,200) from intake below 20 g/day, and 41,300 (35,400–145,800) from intake up to 10 g/day.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The closing paragraph of the discussion says alcohol use “causes a substantial burden of cancer” (Discussion, 9th paragraph), and the authors call their main results “conservative estimates” (6th paragraph). Gaps: (1) causation is an input of the model (IARC's classification), not a finding; (2) 'conservative' is argued only from choices that lower the estimate (IARC sites only; current drinking only), while choices that may raise it, which the authors acknowledge elsewhere (residual confounding by tobacco in the relative risks, no modelling of interactions, counting harms without the inverse kidney association), are not weighed against them; (3) the moderate-drinking figure depends on the low-intake shape of the WCRF relative-risk functions, which the main text does not show, and its interval runs to twice the point estimate; (4) the 'population-based study' label describes a model in which no population was observed; (5) the uncertainty intervals leave out uncertainty in incidence, histological splits, latency, model structure and imputed countries. The policy recommendations (taxation, availability, marketing, labels) are not tested by the model.

timeline.event: IARC monograph volume 100E: sufficient evidence that alcohol causes the cancer sites used in this model.

Praud et al.: 5.5% of new cancer cases worldwide in 2012 attributed to alcohol, with pancreatic and gallbladder cancers (about 40,000 cases) in the main analysis (as cited in this paper's discussion).
WCRF/AICR Continuous Update Project expert report: source of the relative risks for current drinking and of the probable inverse kidney association left out here.

Shield et al.: 4.8% of cancer deaths worldwide in 2016 attributed to alcohol, with former drinking in the main analysis; source of the PAF method and exposure model adapted here (Shield is a co-author).
GBD 2019 risk-factor analysis (Murray et al.): 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2019 attributed to alcohol (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Linked Lancet Oncology comment by Justice, 'Alcohol and the global burden of cancer: what are we missing?' (doi 10.1016/S1470-2045(21)00329-6). Its free first paragraph summarises the estimates and argues that understanding the burden, its mechanisms and how to intervene depends on accurate measures of alcohol exposure; the rest is behind registration and was not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The current reference estimate of alcohol-attributable cancer incidence worldwide (2020). It is close in size to earlier global estimates that used other years, outcomes (deaths rather than cases) and site lists (4.8% to 5.5%), and the authors attribute the differences partly to definitions (hepatocellular carcinoma rather than all liver cancer; former drinking; pancreas and gallbladder) and partly to falling consumption in parts of Europe. Because the estimates share inputs (GISAH exposure data, Shield and colleagues' method, IARC's site list), their agreement is not independent confirmation. Claims should present it as a model estimate under stated assumptions, naming the counterfactual (lifetime abstention), the exposure year (2010) and the category bounds (below 20, 20–60 and above 60 g/day), and should give the interval with the moderate-drinking figure.

funding.funder: As printed: "Funding: None." (Summary); "There was no funding source for this study." (Role of the funding source). The first author's work was done during a PhD studentship at IARC (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: "We declare no competing interests."
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from IARC (Lyon; part of WHO, which holds the copyright), the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto (Shield, Sornpaisarn, Rehm), the Centre for Research and Information on Substance Abuse (Uyo, Nigeria), the American Cancer Society, the Netherlands Comprehensive Cancer Organization and Erasmus MC, Sechenov University and TU Dresden. The PAF method is adapted from co-author Shield's earlier work, the exposure data come from WHO's GISAH, and IARC researchers produced both the incidence estimates and this analysis. No industry ties are stated. Recorded as flags, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Being an estimate, the paper cannot be settled by a single study, but three inputs would make it much firmer: relative-risk functions estimated in prospective cohorts with lifetime abstainers as the reference, by world region and ALDH2 genotype, with repeated and biomarker-validated intake; nationally representative surveys calibrated to sales in each country; and uncertainty intervals that also carry the uncertainty in incidence, histological splits and latency.

domains.note: Incidence from GLOBOCAN 2020 (itself modelled for many countries, no allowance for COVID-19); histological splits from one published study (oesophagus) and unpublished estimates (liver, which supply 154,700 attributable cases); exposure from 2010 per-capita consumption, with survey prevalence corrected for under-reporting but not by age or sex; ten countries imputed from regional averages. Data quality is weakest where unrecorded consumption is high (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

Relative risks for current drinking come from the WCRF systematic reviews (a recognised source) but are not shown in the main text (appendix, not read); their reference group is not stated. One set of curves is applied to every population (no ALDH2 or regional differences), residual confounding by tobacco is acknowledged, and interactions with tobacco, hepatitis viruses, aflatoxin and obesity are not modelled. The moderate-drinking share rests on the low-intake part of these curves.

Lifetime abstention, appropriate for cancers whose risk curves rise from zero intake. Two stated framing choices go with it: former drinkers carry no excess risk in the main analysis (lowers the estimate; sensitivity analysis +25%), and the inverse kidney association is not netted (counts harms only).

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: The 1000 draws cover drinking status, the mean and SD of consumption and the relative risks (Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph). Uncertainty in incidence, histological splits, the 10-year latency, the shape of the intake distribution, the upper limit of 150 g/day and the imputed countries is not included. Several intervals are strongly asymmetric with the point estimate close to the lower limit (moderate 103,100, 82,600–207,200; up to 10 g/day 41,300, 35,400–145,800), which the paper does not explain.

Two sensitivity analyses: adding stomach and pancreas raises the total by 9% (808,700) and adding former drinking by 25% (925,900; editors' arithmetic). No sensitivity analysis for latency, the source of the relative risks, the exposure data or the under-reporting correction; the reported increment for former drinking does not match its own totals (reporting issue 1).

Method and inputs are described clearly in outline, but the relative-risk values, the exposure model and country results sit in a 2 MB appendix; code and inputs are available on request only; one input is unpublished; two arithmetic inconsistencies appear in the main text (reporting issues 1 and 2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for comparative risk assessment models (METHODS §5.3). The domains are the design limits named in the round's brief, judged low, some concerns or high by the editors, with the overall no milder than the worst domain. Most of the headline total comes from intake of 20 g/day or more (86% of attributable cases), where the relative risks for upper aerodigestive, liver and colorectal cancer are large and consistent, so the order of magnitude (about 4% of new cancers) is robust to moderate changes in inputs; former drinking alone would add a quarter. The share attributed to moderate drinking depends on the low-intake shape of relative-risk functions that the main text does not show, and its interval is wide and skewed. The intervals reflect only sampling uncertainty in exposure and relative risks. Cite the paper for the size and distribution (by sex, site, region and intake band) of the modelled alcohol-attributable cancer burden, with its counterfactual and assumptions stated; do not cite it as evidence that alcohol causes cancer, which it assumes.

key_findings.finding: Globally, an estimated 741,300 new cancer cases in 2020 (95% UI 558,500–951,200), 4.1% (3.1–5.3) of all new cancers excluding non-melanoma skin cancer, were attributable to alcohol, against a counterfactual of lifetime abstention: 568,700 in men (76.7%; UI 422,500–731,100; PAF 6.1%, 4.6–7.9) and 172,600 in women (23.3%; 135,900–220,100; PAF 2.0%, 1.6–2.5).
key_findings.locator: Summary › Findings; Results, 1st paragraph; Table (all sites row)

key_findings.finding: The global age-standardised incidence rate of alcohol-attributable cancer was 8.4 per 100,000 (UI 6.2–10.9): 13.4 (10.0–17.4) in men and 3.7 (2.7–5.0) in women.

Highest PAFs by site: oesophagus 31.6% (UI 18.4–45.7), pharynx 22.0% (9.0–37.8), lip and oral cavity 20.2% (12.1–32.3); oesophageal PAF 39.2% (22.7–55.6) in men vs 14.3% (9.0–23.5) in women. Other sites (both sexes): larynx 15.0%, liver 17.3%, rectum 9.0%, colon 8.1%, female breast 4.4% (3.0–5.8).
key_findings.note: For oesophagus and liver, the attributable cases are squamous cell and hepatocellular carcinomas only, but the PAF is a fraction of all oesophageal or liver cancers (Table footnotes).

key_findings.finding: By intake among current drinkers: heavy drinking (above 60 g/day) contributed 346,400 cases (46.7%; UI 227,900–489,400), risky drinking (20–60 g/day) 291,800 (39.4%; 227,700–333,100) and moderate drinking (below 20 g/day, up to about two drinks a day) 103,100 (13.9%; 82,600–207,200).

Intake up to 10 g/day contributed 41,300 cases (UI 35,400–145,800): 16,700 (14,300–75,400) in men, 2.9% of men's attributable cases, and 24,600 (21,100–70,400) in women, 14.3% of women's. The largest numbers of attributable cases were in men drinking 30 to under 50 g/day and in women drinking 10 to under 30 g/day.
key_findings.note: Figure 4 (cases by 10-g/day band) is an image; no values were read from it.

key_findings.finding: The share of attributable cases due to heavy drinking (above 60 g/day) was highest, among men, in southern Africa (2100 of 2800, given as 72.9%) and central and eastern Europe (34,800 of 49,900, 69.7%), and among women in southern Africa (590 of 1400, 43.4%) and western Africa (990 of 2700, 37.2%).
key_findings.note: Printed counts are rounded, so the percentages do not reproduce exactly from them (editors' arithmetic: 2100/2800 = 75.0%).

key_findings.finding: Regional PAFs were lowest in northern Africa (0.3%, UI 0.1–3.3) and western Asia (0.7%, 0.5–1.2) and highest in eastern Asia (5.7%, 3.6–7.9) and central and eastern Europe (5.6%, 4.6–6.6); the highest national PAFs were in Mongolia, China, Moldova and Romania.

Regional age-standardised rates of attributable cancer were highest in men in central and eastern Europe (23.1 per 100,000, UI 19.0–26.6), eastern Asia (21.5), western Europe (17.3) and Australia and New Zealand (17.0), and in women in Australia and New Zealand (10.2, 6.3–15.2), western Europe (9.4) and northern Europe (9.1). The male-to-female ratio ranged from 1.7–1.8 (Australia and New Zealand, northern and western Europe) to 5.6–6.8 (south-central and southeastern Asia).

Sensitivity analyses: including stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700 (UI 616,300–1,034,800; PAF 4.5%), with 50,000 pancreatic (PAF 10.1%) and 17,400 stomach cancer cases (PAF 1.6%); including former drinking added 135,000 (102,200–171,900) cases for a total of 925,900 (705,900–1,187,500; 713,200 men, 212,700 women), PAF 5.2% (3.9–6.6), age-standardised rate 10.3 per 100,000.
key_findings.note: The stated increment and totals do not reconcile: 925,900 − 741,300 = 184,600, not 135,000 (editors' arithmetic); see reporting issue 1. Quote the totals with this caveat.

key_findings.finding: Model structure: Levin-based PAFs with lifetime abstention as the theoretical minimum-risk exposure; intake among current drinkers integrated from 0.1 to 150 g/day; 2010 GISAH exposure assumed to act after 10 years; WCRF relative risks for current drinking; 1000 Monte Carlo-like draws of drinking status, mean and SD of consumption and relative risks, with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% UI.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sites: only cancers with sufficient evidence in IARC monograph 100E; oesophageal and liver cancer restricted to squamous cell and hepatocellular carcinoma; stomach and pancreas only in sensitivity analysis; a probable protective effect on kidney cancer at intakes up to 30 g/day (WCRF) deliberately not included.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The global PAF is lower than earlier estimates of 5.5% of cancer cases in 2012, 4.8% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2019; the authors attribute this to falling consumption in some regions, the use of hepatocellular carcinoma rather than all liver cancer (about 80% of primary liver cancers), sites included, former drinking, and incidence rather than mortality.

Limitations stated by the authors: the under-reporting correction does not vary by age or sex and ignores changes before and after 2010; surveys underestimate former drinking; data quality varies by country; residual confounding by tobacco and no modelling of synergy with tobacco, hepatitis B or C, aflatoxin or obesity; no population-specific relative risks (ALDH2*2 carriers, people with a history of cancer); 2020 incidence not adjusted for COVID-19 disruptions.

reporting_issues.issue: The former-drinking sensitivity analysis is said to add 135,000 cases (UI 102,200–171,900) and to raise the total to 925,900, but 925,900 − 741,300 = 184,600; the sex-specific totals (713,200 + 212,700 = 925,900) imply increases of 144,500 in men and 40,100 in women (editors' arithmetic). Neither the increment nor the total matches 741,300 + 135,000 = 876,300, or the stomach-and-pancreas total of 808,700 plus 135,000.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the increment or the totals are misprinted; the PAF (5.2%) and rate (10.3 per 100,000) fit the total of 925,900 better. Claims about the effect of including former drinking should quote the totals and note the discrepancy.

reporting_issues.issue: Table, pharyngeal cancer row: the male age-standardised rate of 1.8 per 100,000 (UI 0.7–3.1) is about twice what 37,000 attributable cases imply when set against the other male rows (about 41,000–44,000 cases per unit of rate at every other site, against about 20,600 for pharynx; editors' arithmetic). The both-sexes rate, 0.5 with an interval of 0.4–1.6, also sits oddly within its own interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typesetting or transcription error in the rates; the case counts and PAFs in the row agree with the rest of the table. Do not cite the pharyngeal rates without checking the appendix.

reporting_issues.issue: Several uncertainty intervals are strongly asymmetric, with the point estimate close to the lower limit: moderate drinking 103,100 (82,600–207,200), up to 10 g/day 41,300 (35,400–145,800), and up to 10 g/day in men 16,700 (14,300–75,400). The main text does not say how the point estimates relate to the simulated distribution.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The point estimates for low-intake categories lie at the low end of what the model's own simulations allow; claims should give the intervals, not the point estimates alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The hepatocellular carcinoma fractions, which determine the 154,700 attributable liver cancer cases, come from unpublished estimates by the first author.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: An input behind the second-largest site estimate could not be checked when the paper was published.

All sections read, including the Research in context box, the Table with its footnotes, the PAF formula as rendered on the page, data sharing, declaration of interests, acknowledgements and contributors; Figures 1–4 are images and their values were not extracted; the supplementary appendix (PDF) was not read. No correction notice is linked on PMC or on thelancet.com, where the linked articles are the Justice (2021) comment, read in its free first paragraph only, and a 2025 editorial that mentions the paper only as one of the journal's most-downloaded.
